meta.title: Turkish — Sounds and spelling
meta.subtitle: 24 letters, sounds and suffix rules — start here, beside Turkish A1
meta.desc: How Turkish is read and spelled, and how its suffixes change, before or beside the first word: 24 notes, one card each — the 8 vowels (a, e, ı, i, o, ö, u, ü), 8 consonant letters whose sound is not the one an English reader gives them (c, ç, g, ğ, j, r, ş, y), and 8 rules: the circumflex, where the stress falls, the suffixes with e or a (-ler, -lar), the suffixes with i, ı, ü or u, the present in -iyor, the final consonant that softens before a vowel (kitap, kitabı), the suffix whose d becomes t (evde, kitapta), and the question particle mi with de, both written apart. Turkish is spelled as it sounds, so the deck is short; what it holds is what the spelling does not tell an English reader. c is the j of joy (29 of Turkish A1's 538 headwords contain it), ç and ş are ch and sh (40 and 58), ı without a dot is another vowel than i (67), ö and ü are front rounded vowels (27 and 52), ğ is never a g (28), j is the s of measure (2); 243 of the 538 contain at least one of these or a circumflex. AND THE SUFFIXES, which every sentence uses: a Turkish word takes its endings one after another, and each ending's vowel is chosen by the vowel before it. The level decks show the forms — 240 cards of Turkish A1 carry a row of cases, 199 a possessed form, 73 a verb's tenses — and the five rule cards here say what the pattern in those rows is, each with a table of forms read off A1's own cards. The front shows the letter or the ending. The back gives the sound in the International Phonetic Alphabet and the English sound it resembles, then words of the Turkish A1 deck with a speaker beside each, the letter picked out, and the word's own transcription from the dictionary (ˈ stands before the stressed syllable, ː after a long vowel). Say the word, then press the speaker and compare. THE ORDER is the vowels, the consonants, then the rules. At the default of ten new cards a day the deck takes 3 days; it is meant to be studied beside Turkish A1, not finished first. — WHAT IS NOT HERE: nothing is written for this deck. Each sound and each English comparison is a cell of the letter's row in the table of the first page named below, and each sentence under a letter a sentence of that page's notes; the rules are sentences of the three pages, each quotation a paragraph of its own, with a cut marked […]. The letters that sound as an English reader expects (b, d, f, h, k, l, m, n, p, s, t, v, z) have no card. The rule cards show only forms an A1 card shows, so the buffer consonants (araba, arabayı; arabası) and the personal endings of the verb are on the cards and have no rule here: no sentence was found to quote for them. The speaker is your device's Turkish voice reading the example word, so a device without one is silent. — Sounds, English comparisons and notes: Wikipedia, “Turkish alphabet”, revision 1387730069 of 2026-11-25. Rules: Wikipedia, “Turkish phonology”, revision 1384242891 of 2026-11-07; Wikipedia, “Turkish grammar”, revision 1379006387 of 2026-10-07 (all CC BY-SA 4.0). Transcriptions: English Wiktionary, via kaikki.org (CC BY-SA 4.0). Example words, forms and meanings: the Turkish A1 deck on this shelf (English Wiktionary via kaikki.org, CC BY-SA 4.0).

fields.Name: the circumflex
fields.Says: Optional circumflex accents can be used with "â", "î" and "û" to disambiguate words with different meanings but otherwise the same spelling, or to indicate palatalisation of a preceding consonant (for example, while kar /kaɾ/ means 'snow', kâr /caɾ/ means 'profit'), or long vowels in loanwords, particularly from Arabic.Native Turkish words have no vowel length distinction.
fields.Examples:
as in
pekâlâ/pe.caːˈlaː/all right
rüzgâr/ɾyzˈɟaɾ/wind
kar/ˈkaɾ/snow

fields.Name: where the stress falls
fields.Says: In most words the accent comes on the last syllable of the word. This final accent is the default situation, but there are some words, such as place names, foreign borrowings, words containing certain suffixes, and certain adverbs, that have exceptional stress.
fields.Examples:
as in
kitap/ciˈtap/book
çocuk/t͡ʃoˈd͡ʒuk/child
araba/ɑ.ɾɑ.ˈbɑ/car
görmek/ɟøɾˈmec/to see, watch
merhaba/ˈmæɾ.ha.baː/hello, hi

fields.Name: a suffix with e or a
fields.Says: Grammatical suffixes feature vowel harmony, meaning that the vowels of suffixes change to harmonize with the vowel of the preceding syllable.twofold (/e/~/a/): […] Backness is preserved, that is, /e/ appears following a front vowel and /a/ appears following a back vowel. For example, the locative suffix is -de after front vowels and -da after back vowels.
fields.Examples:
as in
ev/ˈev/A building for a family to reside in; house, home, abode.
kız/kɯz/girl

fields.Name: a suffix with i, ı, ü or u
fields.Says: fourfold (/i/~/y/~/ɯ/~/u/): Both backness and rounding are preserved. For example, the genitive suffix is -in after unrounded front vowels, -ün after rounded front vowels, -ın after unrounded back vowels, and -un after rounded back vowels.
fields.Examples:
as in
gün/ˈɟyn/day
okul/oˈkuɫ/school

fields.Name: the present: its o never changes
fields.Says: In the isolated case of /o/ in the verbal progressive suffix -i⁴yor it is immutable, breaking the vowel harmony such as in yürüyor ('[he/she/it] is walking').The first syllable of the imperfective suffix (-iyor) exhibits vowel harmony while the second is invariable. When suffixed to a stem ending in a vowel, that vowel is elided: ye- + -iyor → yiyor.
fields.Examples:
as in
gelmek/ɟelˈmec/to come, move closer
almak/aɫˈmak/to take

fields.Letters: p ç t k → b c d ğ
fields.Name: a final consonant before a vowel
fields.Says: /b, d, d͡ʒ, ɡ, ɟ/ are devoiced to [p, t, t͡ʃ, k, c] word- and morpheme-finally, as well as before a consonant: /edˈmeɟ/ ('to do, to make') is pronounced [etˈmec]. (This is reflected in the orthography, so that it is spelled ⟨etmek⟩). When a vowel is added to nouns ending with postvocalic /ɡ/, it is lenited to ⟨ğ⟩ (see below); this is also reflected in the orthography.
fields.Examples:
as in
kitap/ciˈtap/book
çocuk/t͡ʃoˈd͡ʒuk/child

fields.Name: a suffix's d after a voiceless consonant
fields.Says: Because of assimilation, an initial voiced consonant of a suffix is devoiced when the word it is attached to ends in a voiceless consonant. For example, the locative of şev (slope) is şevde (on the slope), but şef (chef) has locative şefte
fields.Examples:
as in
deniz/deˈniz/sea
sokak[soˈkɑk]street, alley

fields.Name: the question particle, written apart
fields.Says: The interrogative particle (soru eki) is not written as a suffix, but phonetically it is enclitic; in particular, it exhibits vowel harmonyThe following, though written separately, are pronounced as if pre-accenting suffixes, and the stress on the final syllable of the preceding word is more pronounced than usual: de/da ('also', 'even'): elmalar da ('even apples'); mi/mu (interrogative): elmalar mı? ('apples?')

mıback-unrounded vowel harmony: ı, after a and ı
muback-rounded vowel harmony: u, after o and u
müfront-rounded vowel harmony: ü, after ö and ü
